title: kernel-adapter-eval-notes-tensorrt-triton
content:
Status: early experiments + notes. Purpose: capture observed tradeoffs integrating TensorRT and Triton into our GPU serving runtime vs continuing with in-house custom kernels. Focus areas: kernel integration complexity, batching and scheduling interactions, KV cache behavior, quantization/accuracy, deploy iteration speed, and operational failure modes.

Environment and test harness:
- GPUs: AWS p4d.24xlarge (8x A100 40GB) and a local dev DGX (A100 80GB)
- OS/container: Ubuntu 20.04 + CUDA 11.8 + cuDNN 8.3
- Triton versions: 22.09, 23.05 experimental
- TensorRT versions used: 8.6.x, 8.5.x
- Model tested: Llama-ish encoder-decoder prototype (decoder-only small 7B variant adjusted for memory), and a small LLM 2B for latency-sensitive tests
- Baseline: current custom kernels with continuous batching (our runtime v0.9.3 feature branch)
- KV-cache: runtime-managed per-request KV stored in GPU memory; cache sharding disabled for these runs

Key observations (high level):
1) Latency vs throughput tradeoffs
- TensorRT path: best steady-state throughput (tokens/sec) on long sequences due to optimized fused attention kernels and optimized matmuls. End-to-end p95 latency slightly worse on very short sequences when compared to our custom runtime because TensorRT introduces extra compilation/optimization overhead and extra device-to-device synchronization with triton server.
- Triton server layer: simplifies deployment but adds measurable jitter in p99 latency (observed +12-18 ms p99 for short queries) due to its internal request queueing and thread-pool scheduling.
- Custom kernels: lower median latency for single-request low-token workloads; our continuous batching gives better tail latency when batch packing is aggressive and request arrival distribution is bursty.

2) Compile and iteration time
- TensorRT engine build time for a 2B model: 6–12 minutes (FP16); INT8 calibrations add another 20–45 minutes depending on calibration dataset size.
- Triton model repo + batching config iteration: relatively quick (seconds to minutes) but any change that invalidates the TRT engine requires a rebuild. Iteration cost for engineering experimentation is higher with TRT.

3) Quantization and accuracy
- FP16: TensorRT FP16 almost lossless for our validation prompts; minor increases in perplexity for certain attention-heavy prompts but not significant for user-facing generation quality.
- INT8: achievable but brittle; calibration dataset choice heavily impacts correctness. For QA-style prompts, some hallucination increases observed. Custom kernels with QAT pipeline gave slightly more consistent results in our tests but required integration effort.

4) KV cache interaction and memory management
- With TensorRT, KV cache is typically managed as regular tensors inside the engine; resizing or dynamic growth for very long sequences triggers full engine reallocation in some cases (Triton + TRT with dynamic shapes), causing large spikes in latency and memory fragmentation over time.
- Our custom runtime's explicit KV cache abstraction (separate buffers per request with incremental append) handled long-session growth more gracefully and avoided full-engine reallocation.
- Recommendation: if using TRT/TRITON, keep KV cache sizes bounded or adopt a dual-mode where KV cache lives outside of the TRT engine (we prototyped a wrapper where attention kernels read KV from external buffers; correct but required custom kernel hooks).

5) Scheduling interactions
- Triton's internal batching is opaque to our runtime scheduler; we saw double-batching in some cases where our continuous batching and Triton's batching both applied -> unnecessary queueing and increased latency.
- When Triton batching disabled, our scheduler regains control and matches expected p50/p95 numbers.
- TensorRT ensemble models in Triton introduce per-model serialization points that reduce parallelism across models when multiple models share GPU resources.

6) Operational failure modes
- TRT engine corruption: observed rare TRT deserialization crashes on driver upgrade paths; recovery requires engine rebuild and careful orchestration.
- Triton process OOM: because Triton includes model repo manager + server, a misestimated memory limit for TRT engines caused the server to kill processes; logs were noisy and slow to surface root cause.
- Custom kernel path: fewer external process-level failure modes; more surface area in our codebase but failures were more localized and easier to inspect (stack traces inside runtime).

7) Observability and tooling
- Triton exposes model metrics but lacks fine-grained token-level tracing aligned with our existing tracing flags. Need adapters.
- TRT profiling gives low-level kernel timing which is useful for pinpointing hotspots but mapping those to request-level latency requires additional instrumentation (we added a thin shim to sample kernel timestamps per batch).

Design tradeoffs and suggested patterns:
- Hybrid model: use TensorRT for high-throughput, long-sequence inference where compile cost and engine rigidity are acceptable; default to custom kernels for low-latency, interactive workloads and during rapid iteration.
- Externalized KV cache: keep KV cache outside the TRT engine where possible. Implement lightweight kernel adapters that can read KV from external buffers while the main matmul/attention kernels are TRT-accelerated. This reduces engine rebuilds and memory fragmentation.
- Scheduler integration: treat Triton as a device pool, not as an internal scheduler. Disable Triton's internal batching; let our runtime scheduler control batching semantics and use Triton only as an execution backend for compiled engines.
- Canary rollout strategy: when switching user traffic to TRT-backed models, ramp up using dedicated GPU pools to isolate fragmentation/OOM effects; add health probes for engine serialization/deserialization errors.

Concrete TODOs / next experiments:
- Prototype external KV cache adapter with TRT attention kernels: measure p95 and memory fragmentation across long lived sessions (2k+ tokens). (Owner: Priya)
- Run controlled latency experiments toggling Triton batching vs disabled with identical request arrival patterns to quantify double-batching cost at p50/p95/p99 (Owner: Liam).
- Calibration sensitivity study for INT8 on multi-domain prompts, create representative calibration datasets per-customer (Owner: Sofia).
- Build a small test harness for hot-driver upgrade paths that attempts deserializing TRT engines across CUDA minor versions to reproduce the rare crash.

Open questions / discussion items:
- Is the added operational complexity of keeping two execution paths justified by the latency/throughput split observed? How many customers require both?
- Long-term: invest in kernel-level reimplementation of the top TRT fused kernels that matter for our models (attention + rotary + kv handling) vs full TRT dependency — ROI analysis needed.
- Could we upstream a lightweight KV-out-of-engine attention kernel into TensorRT plugin ecosystem to reduce our maintenance burden?

Quick reference commands used in experiments:
- TRT build snippet: trtexec --onnx=model.onnx --workspace=50000 --fp16 --saveEngine=model.trt
- Triton run (disabled batching): tritonserver --model-repository=/models --strict-model-config=false --allow-metrics=true --max-batch-size=1
- Perf harness: python bench.py --clients 64 --qps 200 --seq-len 512 --warmup 30 --duration 120

Appendix: brief benchmark table (representative single-run numbers, small 2B test model):
- Custom kernels (continuous batching): throughput 2200 tokens/s, p50 32ms, p95 78ms, p99 140ms
- TensorRT (direct engine, scheduler-managed batching): throughput 2800 tokens/s, p50 44ms, p95 96ms, p99 170ms
- Triton + TRT (default batching): throughput 2500 tokens/s, p50 52ms, p95 110ms, p99 188ms

Notes: numbers vary by GPU, driver, and exact model shape. These are a starting point for capacity planning and not final benchmarks.

Short-term recommendation: adopt a hybrid approach in beta. Use TRT-backed engines in Dedicated GPU pools for customers that need predictable throughput and are willing to accept longer iteration times. Default hosted tiers and interactive flows should remain on our custom kernel path until we solve KV externalization and scheduling collision issues.

End of notes.
